title: Evaluate external animal anatomy and morphology

lessons.title: Naming the outside parts of farm animals
lessons.html:
Why know the body parts?

Anatomy means the parts of the body. Morphology means the shape and form of the animal. When you know the correct names for body parts you can tell the vet or your supervisor exactly where a wound or swelling is, and you can judge whether an animal is well built for its job.

Main body parts of a cow

  • Head: poll (top of the head), forehead, muzzle, jaw, ears, horns or polled.
  • Neck and front: crest, dewlap (loose skin under the neck), brisket (chest between the front legs), shoulder.
  • Back line: withers (top of the shoulders), back, loin, hip (hook bones), rump, pin bones, tail head.
  • Side and belly: ribs, flank, barrel, belly.
  • Legs: forearm, knee, cannon, fetlock, pastern, hoof (claws), hock on the back leg, stifle.
  • Udder and teats in cows, sheath and scrotum in bulls.

Differences between species

AnimalSpecial features
SheepFleece, breech area, cloven hooves
GoatBeard, often horns, cloven hooves
PigSnout, many teats, cloven feet
HorseSingle solid hoof, mane, frog of the hoof
ChickenComb, wattles, beak, spurs on cocks

Practise naming the parts on the animals you work with every day. Use the names when you report to your supervisor.

lessons.title: Judging body shape and soundness
lessons.html:
Conformation

Conformation is how well the body is built. A well-built animal lives longer, walks further on the veld, breeds better and gives more product. When you look at an animal, look from the side, from the front and from behind, while it stands on flat ground and while it walks.

What to look for

  • Legs and feet: straight legs, strong pasterns, even claws, no limping. Animals with bad legs cannot walk to water and grazing.
  • Back line: strong and level back, not dipped or humped.
  • Body depth: deep chest and wide barrel give room for heart, lungs and rumen.
  • Mouth: teeth must meet the dental pad correctly. Undershot or overshot jaws make grazing hard.
  • Udder and teats: well attached udder, four even teats of good size, no hard lumps.
  • Testes: two even, firm testes of good size in bulls and rams.
  • Eyes: clear, without discharge or growths.

Body condition scoring

Body condition score (BCS) tells you how fat or thin an animal is. Many farms use a scale of 1 to 5 where 1 is very thin and 5 is very fat. Feel the backbone, ribs, hip and tail head with your hand.

ScoreWhat you feel and see
1Bones stick out sharply, no fat
3Bones felt with light pressure, smooth body
5Bones hard to feel, fat lumps at tail head

Both very thin and very fat animals have problems with breeding and birth.

lessons.title: Ageing animals and recording findings
lessons.html:
Telling age by the teeth

Cattle, sheep and goats have no top front teeth. They have a hard dental pad. The front teeth on the bottom jaw change from small milk teeth to broad permanent teeth as the animal grows. Farmers talk about a two-tooth, four-tooth, six-tooth and full-mouth animal.

  • Milk teeth: young animal, small narrow teeth.
  • Two-tooth: the first pair of broad permanent teeth have come out.
  • Four-tooth, six-tooth: more permanent pairs.
  • Full mouth: all eight permanent front teeth.
  • Broken mouth: old animal with worn or missing teeth. It struggles to graze and is often culled.

The exact age at which each pair appears differs by species, breed and feeding, so use the farm's chart.

Handling safely while you inspect

  • Put cattle in a crush. Never stand behind a cow or at the side of the back leg where it can kick.
  • Hold sheep and goats gently by the jaw and the side, not by the wool or horns alone.
  • Open the mouth from the side, keeping your fingers away from the back teeth.
  • Wash your hands after handling animals.

Recording

Write down the animal's number or tag, date, body condition score, teeth, and any faults such as lameness, bad udder, eye problems or wounds. Mark animals with serious faults so that the manager can decide whether to treat, cull or keep them out of breeding.

Key points

  • Anatomy is the body parts; morphology is the shape and form.
  • Use correct names such as withers, brisket, hock and pastern when reporting.
  • Good conformation means sound legs, a strong back, a good mouth and a sound udder or testes.
  • Body condition score shows if an animal is too thin or too fat.
  • Teeth show age: milk teeth, two-tooth up to full mouth and broken mouth.
